main.title: Doctor Pong
main.summary: Doctor Pong, also known as Puppy Pong, is an adaptation of the original arcade Pong for use in a non-coin-operated environment.

cards.heading: Pong enters the waiting room
cards.text: Doctor Pong, also known as Puppy Pong, is an adaptation of the original arcade Pong for use in a non-coin-operated environment. It was conceptualized by Nolan Bushnell, Steve Bristow, and a marketing firm to move their arcade video games into a non-arcade environment—in this case, to help occupy children in pediatricians' waiting rooms. Originally designed to be a model of Snoopy's doghouse with Pong built into the side of it, when Charles Schulz declined Atari the use of Snoopy, the model was changed to a generic doghouse with a puppy looking over the top. Puppy Pong saw a limited production run and was tested at Chuck E. Cheese's Pizza Time Theatre's first two locations.

cards.heading: Designing the doghouse cabinet
cards.text: The original Snoopy Pong cabinet was designed by Regan Cheng of the Atari Industrial Design group. The follow-up Puppy Pong cabinet was designed by Regan's manager, Chas Grossman.

cards.heading: Replacing the coin with a start button
cards.text: Both cabinets consisted of a doghouse housing a Pong board modified to not use a coin drop as a start trigger. The original Pong automatically starts several seconds after a coin is inserted. In Doctor Pong and Puppy Pong, a "start button" was instead wired up to start the games, set under the vertically mounted television in the dog house "roof." Instead of a traditional control panel, spinners are mounted directly on the roof, as well.

main.title: Shark Jaws
main.summary: Shark Jaws is an action video game by Atari, Inc. under the name of Horror Games, originally released for arcades in 1975.

cards.heading: An arcade game in the wake of Jaws
cards.text: Shark Jaws is an action video game by Atari, Inc. under the name of Horror Games, originally released for arcades in 1975. An unlicensed tie-in to the movie Jaws, and believed to be the first commercially released movie tie-in, it was created to be a game about sharks eating people. According to Bushnell, the game was successful enough to sell approximately two thousand units.

cards.heading: A diver, small fish and a larger threat
cards.text: In the game, the player controls a deep-sea diver trying to catch small fish while avoiding a great white shark that is trying to eat him. Points are scored by running over the fish to catch them. The score appears at the top of the screen.

cards.heading: A prominent name without a film licence
cards.text: Atari head Nolan Bushnell originally tried to license the Jaws name, but was unable to secure a license from Universal Pictures. Deciding to go ahead with the game anyway, it was retitled Shark JAWS, with the word Shark in tiny print and JAWS in large all caps print to create greater prominence. Afraid of legal action from Universal, Atari released it under a fake name, Horror Games.

cards.heading: A shark-filled cabinet around Atari circuitry
cards.text: The game is housed in a custom cabinet that includes a single joystick and start button. The cabinet bezel uses blue and green colors, and portrays sharks swimming around along with a solitary swimmer. The game PCB is composed of discrete technology, and although the game was released under the name Horror Games, the PCB clearly states Atari.

main.title: Jerry Lawson and the Channel F team
main.subtitle: One console. A game you have not bought yet.
main.summary: Jerry Lawson and his colleagues helped turn a television game into a platform: keep the machine, change the cartridge.

cards.heading: A new game in a cartridge
cards.text: Fairchild introduced the Channel F in 1976, bringing interchangeable program cartridges to a home television-game system. A household could keep the console and buy further games for it. Each cartridge contained a different program, changing what the machine could play without replacing the whole device.

cards.heading: The team behind the machine
cards.text: Jerry Lawson led engineering work on the system. Fairchild had licensed an earlier design from Alpex, and bringing it into the living room required several kinds of expertise. Lawson's electronics work sat alongside Ron Smith's mechanical engineering and Nicholas Talesfore's industrial design. The cartridge and controller were physical objects that people would repeatedly insert, remove, grip and twist; a successful prototype also had to become something a household could use.

cards.heading: A library that could keep growing
cards.text: The result changed the relationship between a purchase and its future. A console could stay under the television while a library grew around it. New software could extend an existing machine's life, and publishers could sell games to people who already owned the hardware.

cards.heading: Lawson beyond the Channel F
cards.text: Lawson later founded Video Soft, extending his work from engineering into entrepreneurship. As a Black engineer leading work on a formative home-game platform, he held a significant position in the development of consumer video-game technology. His Channel F work brought together the electronic, mechanical and industrial-design contributions of the Fairchild team.

features.title: A cartridge has to survive the living room
features.summary: Interchangeable games required practical decisions about handling, connections and shielding.

cards.heading: From prototype to product
cards.text: Fairchild developed Alpex's cartridge-system design into the Channel F. Jerry Lawson's account describes the practical challenge of making removable games reliable enough for everyday household use. A family would repeatedly insert and remove the cartridges, so the connection and its protection had to work beyond a successful bench demonstration.

cards.heading: Shaping the cartridge
cards.text: Alpex engineers Wallace Kirschner and Lawrence Haskel contributed the earlier design. At Fairchild, Lawson worked with mechanical engineer Ron Smith and industrial designer Nick Talesfore. Talesfore drew on the familiar shape of an eight-track tape for the cartridge's appearance. A spring-loaded protective door helped shield the connection, joining the housing's design to the way users would handle it.

cards.heading: Containing electronic interference
cards.text: Lawson recalled regulatory testing and electronic interference as difficult parts of bringing the console to market. The team surrounded the motherboard with aluminium, added electrical bypasses to connections and placed a metal chute over the cartridge adapter. New cartridges also needed testing. The opening that allowed games to be exchanged was one more part of the system to consider when shielding its electronics.

cards.heading: An independent business
cards.text: Lawson incorporated Video Soft in May 1982, moving into independent game development after his work at Fairchild. Its projects encountered the industry's market contraction and the wider recession, and some were cancelled. The business extended Lawson's career beyond console engineering into the challenges of financing and operating a software company.

features.title: VideoSoft beyond the cartridge
features.summary: Jerry Lawson negotiated room to build his own business.

cards.heading: Working under contract
cards.text: In December 1982, Lawson told Black Enterprise that VideoSoft had begun with four designers and private funding for its first projects. The team had completed three games for larger software companies, although contracts prevented him from naming them. Payment combined a fixed fee with royalties after release. Financing and contract terms determined how the small company could continue its development work.

cards.heading: Plans beyond one room
cards.text: Lawson's plans extended beyond writing another cartridge. The same interview described a Smart Cart system intended to let people compete from home over telephone lines. He was also considering a cheaper cartridge and wanted VideoSoft to manufacture and distribute games itself. These were ambitions described while the business was young. The difference between finishing a program for someone else and reaching customers directly involved more than technical invention. Distribution, production costs and a working connection between distant players all appeared in the company's proposed future.

cards.heading: Changing the work
cards.text: By August 1985, Black Enterprise was asking what happened after the boom. Lawson described a changed VideoSoft, making more hardware designs and application software as the games market contracted. His experience organising Fairchild's game division had encouraged him to work independently, but independence meant adapting the product as customers changed. The follow-up catches an engineer making a business decision in the middle of uncertainty. The company that had sought game contracts was looking for other ways to put its technical skills to work.

cards.heading: Finding the money
cards.text: Money remained a design constraint at the scale of the whole company. Lawson told the magazine that he had underestimated how difficult raising capital would be for a minority technology business. Investors had become wary after the industry's downturn, and a convincing idea did not automatically unlock funding. His proposed response was to make arrangements with larger companies while pursuing unfamiliar technical territory. The decision joined two needs: enough commercial support to continue working, and enough freedom to keep attempting something that other firms had not done.

main.title: Night Driver
main.summary: Night Driver is a 1976 racing video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades.

cards.heading: Building a road from roadside markers
cards.text: Night Driver is a 1976 racing video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades. It is  one of the earliest first-person racing video games and is commonly believed to be one of the first published video games to feature real-time first-person graphics. Night Driver has a black and white display with the hood of the player's car painted on a plastic overlay. The road is rendered as scaled rectangles representing "pylons" that line the edges.

cards.heading: Two cabinets for the night drive
cards.text: Two arcade cabinet styles were manufactured: upright and sit-down. The upright version has a blacklight installed inside the cabinet which illuminated the bezel.

cards.heading: A colour version reaches the VCS
cards.text: Atari published a color version for the Atari Video Computer System in 1980.

cards.heading: Reading bends through a wheel and pedals
cards.text: The player controls a car which must be driven along a road at nighttime without crashing into the sides of the road as indicated by road side reflectors. The game is controlled with a single pedal for the accelerator, a wheel for steering and a four-selection lever for gear shifting. The coin-operated game had a choice of three difficulties (novice, pro and expert), which the player could select at game start. The turns were sharper and more frequent on the more difficult tracks. As play progresses, the road gets narrower and more winding.

cards.heading: Time bonuses reward a learned route
cards.text: The game length is 50, 75, 100, or 125 seconds based on an internal setting. After 300 points, a player is awarded bonus time equal to game time, but the score wraps around back to zero at 1000 points, so it is possible to reach 300 points more than once. Due to the additional points received for more difficult play, playing on the expert setting is actually the easiest to achieve extra time once a player has mastered the game.

cards.heading: The car printed in front of the screen
cards.text: The car the player is driving is not actually drawn in the game, but is printed on plastic insert in front of the monitor.

cards.heading: A cabinet photograph becomes a design brief
cards.text: The development of Night Driver was led by Dave Shepperd at Atari, who was given an assignment to develop a first-person driving video game. Shepperd said that he "was given a piece of paper with a picture of a game cabinet that had a small portion of the screen visible" which he recalls being possibly "a German game" but "never saw the game play" other than "that there were a few little white squares showing". Shepperd used that concept to develop Night Driver. That the car is driving at night provided an excuse for the minimal graphics, as most features (like the street and buildings) aren't visible in the dark. While he did not know the title of the German game at the time, it was later identified as the coin-op Nürburgring 1, a first-person driving video game released earlier in 1976.

main.title: Sea Wolf
main.summary: Sea Wolf is an arcade video game designed by Dave Nutting and released by Midway in 1976.

cards.heading: Looking through the periscope
cards.text: Sea Wolf is an arcade video game designed by Dave Nutting and released by Midway in 1976. It is a video game update of an electro-mechanical Midway game, Sea Devil, itself based on Sega's 1966 electro-mechanical arcade submarine simulator Periscope. The game was released in Japan by Taito. In Sea Wolf, the player, piloting an unseen submarine, launches torpedoes vertically in an attempt to sink ships moving horizontally across the screen before time runs out. The screen is viewed through a faux periscope mounted on the cabinet.

cards.heading: A submarine game finds its audience
cards.text: The game sold 10,000 arcade cabinets and was the highest-grossing arcade video game of 1976 and 1977 in the United States and Japan's fifth highest-grossing arcade video game of 1976.

cards.heading: Colour and home-computer versions follow
cards.text: Midway released a color arcade sequel, Sea Wolf II, in 1978. In 1982, Commodore International produced cartridge ports of Sea Wolf for the VIC-20 and then-new Commodore 64 computers.

main.title: F-1
main.summary: F-1 is a 1976 electro-mechanical arcade racing game developed and published by Nakamura Manufacturing Company (Namco), and distributed in North America by Atari, Inc.

cards.heading: A race made from light and moving models
cards.text: F-1 is a 1976 electro-mechanical arcade racing game developed and published by Nakamura Manufacturing Company (Namco), and distributed in North America by Atari, Inc. The player uses a steering wheel to control a Formula One racer, which must avoid collision with other vehicles. The game uses a miniature diorama with small, plastic cars to represent the player's car and opponents on a physical, rotating track, while also featuring a projector system and lighting tricks to create the illusion of racing.

cards.heading: Designing a smaller mechanical spectacle
cards.text: The game was designed by company engineer Sho Osugi, who worked on many of the company's earlier driving-themed electro-mechanical games, and was made to be a smaller version of his earlier game Formula-X that could easily be placed into smaller stores and entertainment centers. The 1968 electro-mechanical driving game Indy 500 by Kansai Seiki Seisakusho (Kasco) is also believed to be a source of inspiration for the game, likely due to Namco's strong business relationship with Kansai prior to development.

cards.heading: An arcade hit before Pole Position
cards.text: F-1 was widely successful upon release, being praised for its sense of thrill, responsive controls and attractive cabinet design. It is cited as the first game based on Formula One racing and one of Namco's first major arcade hits. It was the highest-grossing arcade game in Japan for two years in a row, in 1976 and 1977, and the highest-grossing electro-mechanical arcade game of 1977 in the United States. It was followed by a sequel, F-1 Mach (1977). A cabinet appears in the film Dawn of the Dead (1978). F-1 later provided the basis for Namco's hit racing video game Pole Position (1982), which was co-designed by Sho Osugi.

main.title: Stunt Cycle
main.summary: Stunt Cycle is an arcade video game by Atari, Inc. released in 1976.

cards.heading: The handlebar becomes the control
cards.text: Stunt Cycle is an arcade video game by Atari, Inc. released in 1976. In the style of the Evel Knievel craze of the mid-1970s, the game allows the player to perform motorcycle jumping stunts. The arcade cabinet is modeled like a motorcycle handlebar, and the player twists the right side for acceleration. The monitor is a 19-inch black and white cathode-ray tube with a black and white overlay. It accommodates 1 player or 2 players alternating.

cards.heading: The jumping challenge reaches home
cards.text: Atari released two dedicated home console versions of Stunt Cycle in 1977.

cards.heading: Three platforms lead to a row of buses
cards.text: The screen is divided into three horizontal platforms connected by tubes on the monitor overlay. The player can only accelerate and brake, with no steering. The motorcycle automatically drives across each platform in sequence: left to right, right to left, then left to right again. The bottom platform has a line of parked buses between two ramps, and the goal is to repeatedly jump the buses and land safely.

cards.heading: A growing line of buses
cards.text: Upon starting, the player must jump over 8 buses. If successful, another bus is added and at 23 buses, one additional credit or crash is added. Otherwise, crashing three times or jumping over 27 buses ends the game.

cards.heading: Carrying enough speed into the jump
cards.text: Accelerating too quickly results in a wheelie and, if speed is not decreased, flipping over backward and crashing. Speed carries over from one platform to the next. On the third platform and thereafter, the cycle must reach the landing ramp to avoid a crash.

cards.heading: Two home units and different chipsets
cards.text: Two dedicated console versions were released by Atari in 1977. Atari's own branded Stunt Cycle version plays four games: a version of the original and three variants (Motocross, Enduro, and DragRace) based on the AY-3-8760 chip by General Instrument. Handlebar grips on the unit allow players to whip, wheelie, and jump up to 32 onscreen buses. The unit provides digital on-screen scoring and color graphics. The Sears Tele-Games version called Motocross Sports Center IV includes the same Stunt Cycle variants and 16 Pong games played with detachable Pong controllers (based on Atari C010765 chip for the Pong games and the GI chip AY-3-8760).

cards.heading: A port changes direction into a television tie-in
cards.text: In 1980, Atari programmer Bob Polaro began to develop a Stunt Cycle port for the Atari 2600 using full color graphics. By the time it was completed, Atari had decided to turn it into a television tie-in game for the Dukes of Hazzard franchise instead. This game never progressed beyond the prototype stage and was not officially released. Bob Polaro independently released 50 copies of Stunt Cycle in 2003.

main.title: Outlaw
main.summary: Outlaw is a 1976 light gun shooter video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades.

cards.heading: A computer-controlled fast-draw opponent
cards.text: Outlaw is a 1976 light gun shooter video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades. The game simulates an Old West fast draw duel between the player and the computer. Outlaw was developed under the name Marshall as a direct response to Midway's Gun Fight (1975). Along with Gun Fight, it was among the earliest Western genre-themed video games.

cards.heading: A duel judged beside Gun Fight
cards.text: Outlaw was released in March 1976. A reviewer in Play Meter compared Outlaw to another Atari arcade release Quiz Show (1976) finding Outlaw to be superior. A retrospective review from Steve Fulton writing for Gamasutra  (now Game Developer) said the game felt dated in comparison to the similarly themed Gun Fight.

cards.heading: The name returns on different games
cards.text: Atari would later publish two other different Western-themed games titled Outlaw which featured different styles of gameplay: Outlaw for the Atari 2600 and Outlaw for iPhone and iPad.

main.title: Tanktics: Computer Game of Armored Combat on the Eastern Front
main.summary: Tanktics: Computer Game of Armored Combat on the Eastern Front is a 1976 two-player tank battle computer wargame by Chris Crawford.

cards.heading: A wargame moves between names and publishers
cards.text: Tanktics began as Chris Crawford's first computer wargame, written for the IBM 1130 in 1976 under the name Wargy I. It simulates tank combat on the Eastern Front, combining a physical map and counters with a computer-controlled opponent. Crawford initially published it himself. An expanded version reached home computers through Avalon Hill in 1981 under the Tanktics name.

cards.heading: Physical counters beside a computer opponent
cards.text: The game has no graphics; the player moves tokens on a physical map to represent a tank battle, with the computer controlling one of the sides.

cards.heading: Critics question the opponent's skill
cards.text: Reviewers criticised the limited ability of the computer opponent. The game's measured pace nevertheless offered an alternative for players seeking less complexity than a detailed board wargame and less immediate action than an arcade game.

cards.heading: Terrain and numbers shape a battle
cards.text: The game simulates a two-player tank battle on a large hex grid. Tanktics has no graphics; the player moves tokens on a map using coordinates the computer, acting as referee, provided. Crawford used maps and tokens from Avalon Hill's Panzer Leader when developing the game. To compensate for the computer's weak artificial intelligence, he gave it twice as many tanks as the player and deleted U-shaped lakes from the map. There are several terrain types: forests, lakes, plains, rough and depressed ground, and also roads which allow much faster movement. There are many types of tanks—different ones for the German and Russian side each—as well as stationary anti-tank guns. At the end of the game, a point system determines whether the player has won or lost the game.

cards.heading: From the IBM 1130 to home computers
cards.text: Crawford created the game, first called Wargy I, in FORTRAN for the IBM 1130 from May to September 1976, reporting that it defeated several experienced war gamers at a December 1976 convention. It was his first video game; he did not sell any copies, which he attributed to the IBM 1130 not being a consumer computer that war gamers would have. He ported it to a KIM-1, then the Commodore PET in December 1978. Crawford sold the PET version himself; as this version was programmed in BASIC, it was easy to port from one system to the other. By 1981, the game had been expanded and renamed into Tanktics, and was published by Avalon Hill under that name for the TRS-80, Apple II, and Atari 8-bit computers.

cards.heading: A measured alternative to arcade action
cards.text: Computer Gaming World in 1982 reported that Tanktics's computer opponent was not as intelligent as the manual claimed, advising players to give themselves "poorer tanks" once they began beating it often. While disliking how the game handled line of sight, and bugs in the Apple II version (the review offered unofficial patches for the BASIC source code), the magazine recommended it for those seeking neither arcade action nor the complexity of Avalon Hill's Panzer games or Squad Leader. A 1991 survey in the magazine of strategy and war games gave Tanktics two and a half stars out of five.

main.title: Fonz
main.summary: Fonz is Sega's 1976 arcade motorcycle-racing game based on the Happy Days character, developed from its Road Race and motorcycle variants.

cards.heading: Racing games meet a television character
cards.text: Fonz is a 1976 arcade motorcycle-racing game by Sega, using Fonzie, Henry Winkler's character from Happy Days. Sega's Road Race appeared in February, followed by the motorcycle variants Man T.T. in August and Moto-Cross. These were rebranded as Fonz in November with a Paramount Television licence. Sega was then owned by Gulf+Western, which also owned Paramount. The arcade game's promotion connected the television character with motorcycle controls and a race against the clock.

cards.heading: A second rider joins the cabinet
cards.text: A two-player version of Man T.T. called Twin Course T.T. was released in January 1977.

cards.heading: Perspective and collision feedback
cards.text: Moto-Cross / Fonz is an early black-and-white motorbike racing game, most notable for introducing an early three-dimensional third-person perspective. Both versions of the game display a constantly changing forward-scrolling road and the player's bike in a third-person perspective where objects nearer to the player are larger than those nearer to the horizon, and the aim was to steer the vehicle across the road, racing against the clock, while avoiding any on-coming motorcycles or driving off the road. The game also introduced the use of haptic feedback, which caused the motorcycle handlebars to vibrate during a collision with another vehicle.

cards.heading: Logic chips, graphics ROM and a tape deck
cards.text: Fonz uses discrete logic, with more than 40 TTL integrated circuits. A ROM chip stores images of the motorcycle in different positions, while a tape deck plays recorded engine and crash sounds. The system changes its internal clock frequency on each scanline to produce changes in the apparent size of objects.

cards.heading: Riding through the handlebar controls
cards.text: The general premise has the player controlling Fonzie on a motorcycle with handlebars on the cabinet.

cards.heading: Balancing speed, steering and collision
cards.text: The player has to go as fast as possible without skidding off the road or colliding with other racing bikes on the screen. Turn the handlebars, and the bike will corner and bank. Twist the handle throttle open, and it will accelerate. When a collision with another bike occurs, the handlebars vibrate and the screen flashes a reverse image. To increase the challenge, the size of the bike can be regulated by the operator.

cards.heading: Related versions reach different markets
cards.text: In Japan, Road Race was among the top twenty highest-grossing arcade video games of 1976, according to the first annual Game Machine chart. In North America, Road Race was reported to be doing strong business upon release. Man T.T. was among the top ten highest-grossing arcade video games of 1977 in Japan.

cards.heading: Sega presents the television tie-in
cards.text: Fonz was introduced at Chicago's Music Operators Association (MOA) show in November 1976. It was the first time that a television character was licensed for a video game, with Sega co-founder David M. Rosen predicting the start of a new coalition between the show business and amusement arcade industries. Sega also advertised the game for having both the road and bikes seen in "true perspective on the game screen, while the player operates realistically functioning handle-bars to simulate high-speed competition riding complete with authentic motor sounds". Sega said the response to the game at the MOA show was "unanimous and enthusiastic" and that test location results were very positive. At the start of December 1976, Sega of America reported that it had manufactured several hundred Fonz arcade cabinets.
